misconceptions.name: Half-Lens Blocking Fallacy
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: If the upper or lower half of a converging lens (or mirror) is covered with opaque black paper, only half of the image of the object will be formed on the screen.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: Every single point on an object emits or reflects an infinite cone of light rays toward all parts of the lens aperture. The uncovered half of the lens still refracts rays from every point of the object to form a complete, intact image in the exact same focal position; only the total luminous flux (brightness/intensity) is reduced by half.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Holistic / pictorial projection thinking: confusing the lens surface with a photographic stencil or window through which the object is seen.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: Student selects that 'half of the object will disappear from the image' or that 'the top/bottom half of the image is cut off'.
literature_citations: Goldberg, F. M., & McDermott, L. C. (1987). An investigation of student understanding of the real image formed by a converging lens or concave mirror. American Journal of Physics, 55(2), 108-119.
Galili, I., & Hazan, A. (2000). Learners' knowledge in optics: interpretation, structure and analysis. International Journal of Science Education, 22(1), 57-88.

misconceptions.name: Screen Reification / Image Exists Only on Screen
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: A real optical image does not exist in three-dimensional space unless a white screen or physical surface is placed exactly at the focal plane to 'catch' or materialize it.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: A real image is defined by the physical convergence of refracted or reflected light rays at specific spatial coordinates. The image exists as an optical field in space whether a screen is present or not; placing an eye behind the focal point in line with the diverging cones allows direct observation of the aerial image.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Classroom lab experiences where images are demonstrated by sliding cardboard screens onto optical benches, creating an artifact of experimental presentation.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: Student claims that removing the screen causes the rays to vanish or prevents the image from forming in space.
literature_citations: Galili, I. (1996). Students' conceptual change in elementary optics. International Journal of Science Education, 18(7), 847-868.

misconceptions.name: Virtual Image Ray Convergence Fallacy
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: Light rays actually travel behind a plane mirror or diverging lens, passing physically through the virtual focal point or virtual image location.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: In virtual image formation, reflected or refracted light rays physically diverge. They never cross behind the mirror or lens; they only appear to diverge from a virtual point when traced backward linearly by the observer's visual system. No light energy reaches behind the mirror.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Solid lines drawn behind mirrors in uncareful student sketches; taking geometric dotted construction lines as physical energy paths.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: Student asserts that a virtual image can be captured by placing photographic paper behind a plane mirror, or draws solid arrowed rays propagating behind the reflecting surface.
literature_citations: Driver, R. et al. (1994). Making Sense of Secondary Science (Chapter on Light).

misconceptions.name: Cartesian Sign Convention Spatial Inversion
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: Object distance (u) or focal length (f) is positive because distance is a scalar measure of length, or assigning signs based on colloquial 'left vs right' without reference to the direction of incident light.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention (NCERT): all distances are measured from the pole (P) of the mirror or optical centre (O) of the lens. Distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive; opposite to incident light are negative. For standard diagrams with light moving left-to-right: u is always negative, f_concave is negative, f_convex is positive.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Algebraic arithmetic habits where real positive physical lengths (e.g., 'object is placed at 20 cm') are plugged directly into 1/f = 1/v - 1/u as u = +20 cm.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: In numerical problems, student substitutes u = +20, leading to erroneous positive or inverted v values, or asserts convex mirror focal length is negative.
literature_citations: CBSE Class 10 Board Examinations Examiners' Report on Common Candidate Errors (Physics - Optics Numerical Problems, 2019-2023).

misconceptions.name: Glass Slab Emergent Ray Angular Deviation Fallacy
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: When a ray of light passes obliquely through a parallel-sided rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is permanently bent at an angle relative to the original incident ray.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: Because the opposing refracting faces of a rectangular glass slab are strictly parallel, the angle of incidence at the first interface equals the angle of emergence at the second interface (i = e). The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, undergoing only lateral displacement, with zero net angular deviation.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Conflating refraction in a parallel-sided slab with refraction through a non-parallel triangular glass prism.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: Student predicts that light emerges tilted away from the initial trajectory or draws an emergent ray not parallel to the incident ray.
literature_citations: NCERT Class 10 Science Textbook (Chapter 9, Activity 9.10); NCERT Exemplar Physics Optics Section.

misconceptions.name: Special Ray Exclusivity / Ray Reification
misconceptions.naive_mental_model: Only the 2 or 3 principal rays shown in textbook ray diagrams (parallel to principal axis, through focus, through optical centre/center of curvature) physically exist or form the image. If one of these specific paths is obstructed, that part of the image disappears.
misconceptions.scientific_ground_truth: An infinite number of rays radiate in all directions from every single point on an illuminated object. The standard rays in textbooks are purely convenient geometric construction tools chosen for their readily predictable paths, not privileged physical entities.
misconceptions.cognitive_trigger: Rote memorization of textbook ray diagrams without ontological understanding of light propagation.
misconceptions.distinguishing_signature: Student claims that an image cannot form if a small pinhole blocks the central optical axis, or believes only 2 rays hit the lens.
literature_citations: Goldberg, F. M., & McDermott, L. C. (1987). An investigation of student understanding of the real image formed by a converging lens or concave mirror.
